newsitem.title: USA: Times: U.S. Rep. Burton accepts favor from AT&T.
newsitem.headline: Times: U.S. Rep. Burton accepts favor from AT&T.

text.p: The Congressman who heads the committee leading the investigation into Democratic fund-raising practices accepted a favor from a corporation whose federal contracts he oversees, the New York Times reported Sunday.

Rep. Dan Burton, chairman of the House Committee on Government Reform and Oversight, asked AT&T to let him play in the Pebble Beach National Pro-Am Tournament, the Times said. AT&T allowed Burton, an Indiana Republican, to play, fulfilling a lifelong dream, the Times said.
His committee, in addition to looking into allegations that Democrats traded access for campaign contributions, handles the federal government's $5 billion in telecommunications contracts.
"I tell you right now I would not sell my vote for anything; and second, I would not sell my vote for a couple rounds of golf," Burton told the Times.
Burton said that he had asked AT&T to play at its tournament several times since 1986. He served on the committee since early 1995. He told the Times that the company agreed last August.
AT&T told the Times that it invited him to the January tournament before he became chairman.
Burton defended his playing at the event to the Times, saying AT&T did not fly him out to California; the trip was paid for with personal and campaign money.
"I presume they were interested in me because of my position," he told the Times. "If I thought that in any way it would have influenced me, I would not have participated in the tournament."
The day before the tournament, Burton played a round of golf with AT&T chairman and chief executive officer Robert Allen, the Times said.
Burton told the Times he did not talk business with Allen, only golf.

The Times reported that interviews and internal documents obtained by the newspaper show that the company had a larger plan to develop relationships with a number of federal officials involved in federal phone contracts.

The documents showed AT&T was also interested in Robert Woods, commissioner of the Federal Telecommunications Service. Woods told the Times that several AT&T lobbyists invited him to dinner at a convention, but he refused.
